messages.subject: boxplot confidence intervals
messages.body_plain:
Dear list members,

I´ve got some questions regarding computations with regard to the 
"boxplot" command:

(1) How does the computation of confidence intervals for the median in 
"boxplot" work?

(1a) Are the C.I.´s estimated using bootstrapping?

(2) Would it also be possible to indicate  least significant difference 
bars  in a boxplot graph?

(3) How can I conclude from looking at the C.I.´s whether two medians 
are significantly different from one another?

I´m using S-Plus 6.1 Professional with

boxplot(split(A,B),confint=T,confnotch=F,confdensity=25,confcol=-1,boxcol=0,subset=C>0)

where A and C are numeric and B is categorical.

Best regards, and many thanks for any suggestions,
Chris.

messages.subject: Re: boxplot confidence intervals
messages.body_plain:
On Mon, 1 Mar 2004, Christoph Scherber wrote:

> I´ve got some questions regarding computations with regard to the 
> "boxplot" command:

This is boxplot.default(), and if you look at the code you will see it is 
mainly a call to an S2 graphics function, that is one predating S-PLUS.

> (1) How does the computation of confidence intervals for the median in 
> "boxplot" work?

Without seeing the code, we don't know.  The standard approach is based on 
asymptotic normality, and the asymptotic variance depends on the pdf of 
the underlying distribution at the median (e.g. MASS4, p.133).  There are 
lots of ways to estimate the latter.

> (1a) Are the C.I.´s estimated using bootstrapping?

Very unlikely given the age of the code, which is probably from the early 
1980's.  Doing it via bootstrapping can be rather tricky (see the example 
in MASS).

> (2) Would it also be possible to indicate  least significant difference 
> bars  in a boxplot graph?

You can add to boxplots.  It is not clear to me what you mean by
LSDs, though which usually apply to group *means* in balanced one-way
layouts.

> (3) How can I conclude from looking at the C.I.´s whether two medians 
> are significantly different from one another?

Not really (and they are only approximate CIs, anyway).  Why would you 
want to compare medians, which are a rather inefficient measure of central 
tendency?

You can conclude something if the two CIs do not overlap, as if there is 
no difference the common true value is contained in both CIs with 
probability 0.95^2.

> I´m using S-Plus 6.1 Professional with
> 
> boxplot(split(A,B),confint=T,confnotch=F,confdensity=25,confcol=-1,boxcol=0,subset=C>0)
> 
> where A and C are numeric and B is categorical.

I don't see a `subset' argument for boxplot, either in the documentation 
or in the code.  Where did you get that from?

--

messages.subject: All combinations of dimensions -SUMMARY-
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Spencer Graves and Bert Gunter for their quick and helpful
reply. Here are the suggestions:

You will get prod(dim(M)-1) 3-dimensional arrays.  What do you want
to do with these 3-d arrays?  At least at the prototype stage, I might
use "for" loops.

 > M <- array(1:27, dim = c(3, 3, 3))
 > M.sum <- array(NA, dim = dim(M) - 1)
 > for(i in 1:2)
    for(j in 1:2)
        for(k in 1:2)
            M.sum[i, j, k] <- M[ - c(i, i + 1),  - c(j, j + 1),
                 - c(k, k + 1)]
 > M

, , 1
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    4    7
[2,]    2    5    8
[3,]    3    6    9

, , 2
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]   10   13   16
[2,]   11   14   17
[3,]   12   15   18

, , 3
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]   19   22   25
[2,]   20   23   26
[3,]   21   24   27
 > M.sum

, , 1
     [,1] [,2]
[1,]   27   21
[2,]   25   19

, , 2
     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    9    3
[2,]    7    1

      hope this helps.  spencer graves
Gentlemen:

>I've been
>told to avoid using for loops because S is very slow. Is there a way
>to vectorize this calculations by treating the data as a whole?

This is, alas, an all too common canard. For loops only slow down
appreciably when the number of loops is very large; in ordinary situations
of the kind you describe, they are generally quite fast, and certainly as
fast as or faster than the apply() family.

Of course, if you can vectorize the calculations, thus shifting the looping
to C code, you will be much faster. However, whether a calculation finishes
in 2 seconds or .2 seconds is usually inconsequential; so don't get too hung
up on this.

(The principal advantage of apply()-ing is code transparency, not speed).

Cheers,

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

(Almost)Always I have written S-PLUS code where for() loop looked indispensable to ME. Since it did my job at the expense of slightly more dos time, I never looked at the alternatives. But, this time I have a very simple problem and I thought for() loop should be able to do the job. But it didn't! 

I am doing one permutation experiment that requires me to analyze data from 500,000 patients(9 samples per patient) and all I want to fit is the linear regression model and extract the estimates of slope on each patient. After running my computer for 16 hrs (CPU usage looked like it was computing all the time), S-PLUS reached patient number 19,000…...Is there any quicker way of doing this in S-PLUS? Or from what I always hear---- S-PLUS is limited by its ability to handle huge datasets at hand, do I have to look for some other software that can do this huge computational task really quickly? Any recommendations?

LOOP:

Nsub<-500,000

for (i in 1:nsub)   

        { od.fit<-lm(data.y~data.x,data="">

        slope[i,]<-coe(od.fit)[2}}

                

Thanks much,

Pravin

Pravin Jadhav

Not at all.  You have not tell S-PLUS that you want the dimension of M to
become 5x4.  Just by adding two of the rows you do not collapse the rows.
(I missed this part of your original post.  Sorry.)  You need to explicitly
remove the row you don't want, e.g., by 

M <- M[-5,]

On a different tack, another way to keep track of complex results is to use 
tapply. In the example below, tapply returns a 3d array of lists, each list 
containing a single component which is itself a 3d array!

> M <- array(1:64, dim = c(4, 4, 4))
> tmp <- expand.grid(i = 1:3, j = 1:3, k = 1:3)
> res <- tapply(1:nrow(tmp), tmp, function(n)
{
        i <- tmp$i[n]
        j <- tmp$j[n]
        k <- tmp$k[n]
        M[ - c(i, i + 1),  - c(j, j + 1),  - c(k, k + 1)]
}
)
> dim(res)
[1] 3 3 3
> class(res[1, 1, 1])
[1] "list"
> res[1, 1, 1]
[[1]]:

     [,1] [,2] 
[1,]   43   47
[2,]   44   48

, , 2

[2,]   60   64

efficiently. "lm" does a lot of things that you only really need to do

slope[i,] <- coef(this.lm)[2]
}

Page 61 of S Poetry has a bit on this.

messages.subject: Re: S-PLUS Vs some other softwares
messages.body_plain:
As 
Andy said, lmList will probably do what you want, but as it uses lm(), it may 
also take a while. If you wish to do it "by hand" yourself, try by() [which is
a 
wrapper for tapply()] and use lsfit instead of lm. As others have 
said, lm may incur a lot of overhead. The code would be something 
like

 

results<- by(the.data.frame, 
the.data.frame$patientID,function(z)coef(lsfit(z$x,z$y))[2] 
)

 

where 
x and y are the x and y values for each patient (note they are in the reverse 
order of lm() syntax, which would be lm(y~x)).

 

results is an object of class "by" -- essentially a list of slopes
of length the number of different patient id's + some additional attribute
info. 
You can probably ignore this.

 

Let
us 
know how this all works out for you. Specifically, did any of the suggestions 
give you an answer in a "reasonable" amount of time, where you define 
"reasonable." Large data sets **CAN** be a problem, but 500,000 x8 with 
little covariate info doesn't sound all that large really, especially
these 
days.

 

Cheers,

messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Dimitris Rizopoulos and Sam Buttrey who suggested the use 
of split and lapply (or sapply).  My original question is:

I have a very large cohort data that contains repeated measures. The 
data looks like:

id   days  event
1     0     0
1    30     0
1    50     0
1    95     1
1   120     1
1   147     0
1   180     0
2     0     0
2    75     0
2   100     0
3     0     0
3    37     1
3    80     1

I need help in finding the following survival times:
 1. For each subject, find the first day that event=1.
 2. If a subject never has event=1, then the last day is used with
    an indicator of censoring (say, censor=1).

For the above data, I expect to obtain:

id  days  censor
1    95      0
2   100      1
3    37      0

The next question bothers me more. Now I restrict to only subjects who
have ever had event=1 (in this example, only subjects 1 and 3). How can
I find the how many days it takes for the subject to return to event=0?
As before, if a subject never returns to event=0, the last observation
day is used with an indicator of censoring. In the above data, I expect
to get

id  days  censor
1   52     0
3   43     1

Here is the solution from Dimitris Rizopoulos in finding the first date 
of (event=1)

data<- c(1, 0, 0,
1,    30,     0,
1,    50,     0,
1,    95,     1,
1,   120,     1,
1,   147,     0,
1,   180,     0,
2,     0,     0,
2,    75,     0,
2,   100,     0,
3,     0,     0,
3,    37 ,    1,
3,    80 ,    1)
> data<- matrix(data,ncol=3,byrow=T)
> data<- as.data.frame(data)
> names(data)<- c("id","days","event")
> out <- matrix( unlist( lapply(split(data, data$id), function(x){
+              if   (all(x$event==0)) return(x[nrow(x),])
+              else return(x[which(x$event==1)[1],])} ) ), ncol=3, byrow=T)
> #out[,3] <- ifelse(out[,3]==1, 0, 1)
> dimnames(out) <- list(NULL, c("id", "days", "censor"))
> out<- as.data.frame(out)
> out$censor<- 1-out$censor
>  out
 id days censor
1  1   95      0
2  2  100      1
3  3   37      0

Below is my code to compute the number of days of returning to (event=0) 
after experiencing (event=1) by adapting Dimitris Rizopoulos' code:

> n.visit<- table(data$id)  #total number of visit
> data$days1<- data$days-rep(out$days, times=n.visit)
> data1<- data[data$days1>0,]
> data1$event<- 1-data1$event
> data1$days<- data1$days1
> data1<- data1[,1:3]
>
> out2 <- matrix(
+         unlist(
+          lapply(split(data1, data1$id), function(x){
+              if   (all(x$event==0)) return(x[nrow(x),])
+              else return(x[which(x$event==1)[1],])}
+                )
+               ), ncol=3, byrow=T)
> dimnames(out2) <- list(NULL, c("id", "days", "censor"))
> out2<- as.data.frame(out2)
> out2$censor<- 1-out2$censor
> out2
 id days censor
1  1   52      0
2  3   43      1

Thank you all for your helps!

Regards,
Peng Huang

Dimitris Rizopoulos wrote:

>     BertG> a wrapper for tapply()] and use lsfit instead of
>     BertG> lm. As others have said, lm may incur a lot of
>     BertG> overhead. The code would be something like
>  
>     .................
> 
> I think it should be lm.fit() , not lsfit().
> This will use the numerical engine below lm() without
> the overhead of formula -> model.frame -> model.matrix.
> 
> Martin Maechler <maechler at stat.math.ethz.ch>  http://stat.ethz.ch/~maechler/

A slightly faster approach may be to use the following function which is
part of the Hmisc library. The S-Plus version is shown below.  x is a
matrix, y a vector.

lm.fit.qr.bare <- function(x, y, 
                          tolerance = .Machine$single.eps, 
                          intercept=TRUE, xpxi=FALSE) {

  if(intercept) x <- cbind(1,x)
  if(storage.mode(x) != "double") storage.mode(x) <- "double"
  if(storage.mode(y) != "double") storage.mode(y) <- "double"
  dx <- dim(x)
  dn <- dimnames(x)
  qty <- y
  n <- dx[1]
  n1 <- 1:n
  p <- dx[2]
  p1 <- 1:p
  dy <- c(n, 1)
  z <- .Fortran("dqrls",
                         qr = x,
                         as.integer(dx),
                         pivot = as.integer(p1),
                         qraux = double(p),
                         y,
                         as.integer(dy),
                         coef = double(p),
                         residuals = y,
                         qt = qty,
                         tol = as.double(tolerance),
                         double(2 * p),
                         rank = as.integer(p))
  coef <- z$coef
  if(length(dn[[2]])) names(coef) <- dn[[2]]
  res <- z$residuals
  sse <- sum(res^2)
  sst <- sum((y-mean(y))^2)

  res <- list(coefficients=coef, residuals=res, 
              rsquared=1-sse/sst, fitted.values=y-res)
  if(xpxi) {
      R <- (z$qr)[p1, , drop = FALSE]
      R[lower.tri(R)] <- 0
      rinv <- solve(R, diag(length(coef)))
      xpxi <- rinv %*% t(rinv)
    res$xpxi <- xpxi
  }
  res
}

I use this for bootstrapping, etc.

Frank

messages.subject: Re: question on nls
messages.body_plain:
Recall that nls assumes normal, independent errors.  Thus, the 
likelihood is

     prod( (1/(sigma*sqrt(2*pi))*exp(-0.5*(resid[i]/sigma)^2)). 

Therefore, the log(likelihood) is

     (-0.5)*( N*log(2*pi*sigma^2) + sum(resid[i]^2)/sigma^2). 

     You can somehow get the MLE of "sigma", plug this into this 
formula, and get the log(likelihood).  The AIC is 
(-2)*(log(likelihood)+k), where k = number of parameters estimated, 
including sigma. 

     I don't know the simplest way to get this, and I don't have time 
to play with it, but ?nls contains a pointer to ?nls.object.  The latter 
says it has a component "residuals".  From this, you can compute "sigma" 
= sum(residuals^2)/N, where N = total number of observations.  NOTE:  
You want to use the MLE here, not (N-k) for the unbiased estimate. 

     There is probably a much easier way to get this, but I can't think 
of it right now. 

     hope this helps. 
     spencer graves

messages.body_plain:

I am trying to run a zero-inflated Poisson model (see attached) and have
only found scripts available for R, and these only give log likelihood
in the output, not residual and null deviance. I was wondering if:

zeroinfl <- function(formula,data=list(),
                     link="logit",
                     count="poisson",
                     method="BFGS",trace=FALSE,maxit=50000,
                     x=FALSE,y=FALSE,model=TRUE,
                     na.action=na.omit,
                     ...)
{
  cat("Zero-Inflated Count Model\n")
  if(link=="probit"){
    linkfn <- pnorm
    cat("Using probit to model zero vs non-zero\n")
  }
  else{
    linkfn <- plogis
    cat("Using logit to model zero vs non-zero\n")
  }

  zeroinflPoisson <- function(parms){
    gamma <- parms[1:k]
    beta <- parms[(k+1):(2*k)]
    
    mu <- Z%*%gamma
    bb <- X%*%beta

    lambda <- exp(bb)

    arg1 <- log(exp(mu) + exp(-lambda))
    arg1 <- arg1[y==0]

    arg2 <- y*bb - lambda
    arg2 <- arg2[y>0]

    arg3 <- log(1 + exp(mu))

    arg4 <- lgamma(y+1)
    arg4 <- arg4[y>0]

    llh <- sum(arg1) + sum(arg2) - sum(arg3) - sum(arg4)
    llh
  }

  NegBin <- function(y,lambda,theta){
    arg1 <- gamma(theta + y)/(gamma(y+1)*gamma(theta))
    r <- lambda/(lambda+theta)
    arg2 <- (1-r)^theta
    arg3 <- r^y
    out <- arg1*arg2*arg3
    out
  }

  LogNegBin <- function(y,lambda,theta){
    arg1 <- lgamma(y+theta)-lgamma(y+1)-lgamma(theta)
    arg2 <- theta*(log(theta)-log(theta+lambda))
    arg3 <- y*(log(lambda)-log(theta+lambda))
    out <- arg1+arg2+arg3
    out
  }
  
  zeroinflNegBin <- function(parms){
    gamma <- parms[1:k]
    beta <- parms[(k+1):(2*k)]
    theta <- exp(parms[(2*k)+1])
    
    mu <- Z%*%gamma
    lambda <- exp(X%*%beta)

    ## logit for y=0
    f0 <- linkfn(mu)
    p0 <- f0 + (1-f0)*(theta/(theta+lambda))^theta
    p0 <- p0[y==0]
    
    ## negbin for y>0

    p1 <- (1-f0)*NegBin(y,lambda,theta)
    p1 <- p1[y>0]
    #lp1 <- log(1-f0) + LogNegBin(y,lambda,theta)
    #lp1 <- lp1[y>0]
    
    ## log-likelihood
    llh <- sum(log(p0)) + sum(log(p1))
    llh
  }

  if(count=="poisson"){
    cat("Using Poisson for counts\n")
    llhfunc <- zeroinflPoisson
  }
  if(count=="negbin"){
    cat("Using Negative Binomial for counts\n")
    llhfunc <- zeroinflNegBin
  }
  
  if (method=="Nelder-Mead")
    control <- list(maxit=maxit,trace=trace,REPORT=1,fnscale=-1)
  if(method=="BFGS")
    control <- list(trace=trace,maxit=maxit,fnscale=-1)
  if(method=="L-BFGS-B")
    control <- list(trace=trace,maxit=maxit,fnscale=-1)
  
  ret.x <- x
  ret.y <- y
  mf <- cl <- match.call(expand.dots=FALSE)
  mf$count <- mf$method <- mf$model <- mf$x <- mf$y <- mf$link <- mf$trace <- 
NULL
  mf$drop.unused.levels <- TRUE
  mf[[1]] <- as.name("model.frame")
  mf <- eval(mf, sys.frame(sys.parent()))
  if (method == "model.frame")
    return(mf)
  mt <- attr(mf,"terms")
  xvars <- as.character(attr(mt, "variables"))[-1]
  if((yvar <- attr(mt, "response")) > 0) xvars <- xvars[-yvar]
  xlev <-
    if(length(xvars) > 0) {
      xlev <- lapply(mf[xvars], levels)
      xlev[!sapply(xlev, is.null)]
    }
  if (length(list(...)))
    warning(paste("Extra arguments", deparse(substitute(...)),

                  "are just disregarded."))
  y <- model.response(mf, "numeric")
  w <- model.weights(mf)
  offset <- model.offset(mf)
  if(!is.null(offset) && length(offset) != NROW(y))
    stop(paste("Number of offsets is", length(offset),
               ", should equal", NROW(y), "(number of observations)"))
  
  if (is.empty.model(mt)) {
    x <- NULL
  }
  else {
    x <- model.matrix(mt, mf, contrasts)
  }
  
  if(is.null(y))
    stop("No observations in y")

  n <- length(y)
  tab <- table(y,exclude=NULL)
  cat("dependent variable y:\n")
  print(tab)
  y0 <- sort(unique(y))           ## unique values of y
  m <- length(y0)                 ## number of unique values
  if(any(floor(y0)!=y0))
    stop("Non-integer values of y encountered, invalid for zeroinfl/count 
model\n")
  if(min(y0)!=0)
    stop("Minimum value of y is not zero, invalid for zeroinfl/count model\n")

  Z <- x
  X <- x
  k <- dim(X)[2]

  
  ## start values
  model0 <- glm(I(y==0)~-1+Z,
                family=binomial)
  g0 <- coef(model0)
  model1 <- glm(y~-1+X,
                family=poisson)
  g1 <- coef(model1)
  stval <- c(g0,g1)
  if(count=="negbin")
    stval <- c(stval,0)

  #stval <- stval0
  
  foo <- optim(fn=llhfunc,
               par=stval,
               method=method,
               control=control,
               hessian=T)
  if(foo$convergence != 0)
    stop("optimization failed to converge")
  
  out <- list()
  out$stval <- stval
  out$par <- foo$par
  out$theta <- NULL
  if(count=="poisson")
    names(out$par) <- c(dimnames(Z)[[2]],dimnames(X)[[2]])
  if(count=="negbin"){
    names(out$par) <- c(dimnames(Z)[[2]],dimnames(X)[[2]],"log(theta)")
    out$theta <- exp(out$par["log(theta)"])
  }
  out$hessian <- foo$hessian
  out$call <- cl
  out$method <- method
  out$count <- count
  out$llh <- foo$value
  if(ret.y)
    out$y <- y
  if(ret.x)
    out$x <- X
  out$link <- link
  out$linkfn <- linkfn
  out$n <- n
  out$k <- k
  class(out) <- "zeroinfl"
  out
}

summary.zeroinfl <- function(obj){
  out <- list()
  out$call <- obj$call
  out$y <- obj$y
  out$n <- obj$n
  out$k <- obj$k
  out$count <- obj$count
  out$gamma <- obj$par[1:obj$k]
  out$beta <- obj$par[(obj$k+1):(2*obj$k)]
  out$theta <- obj$theta
  out$vc <- -solve(obj$hessian)
  out$se <- sqrt(diag(out$vc))
  out$coefficients <- cbind(obj$par,
                            out$se)
  tstat <- out$coefficients[,1]/out$coefficients[,2]
  pval <- 2*pnorm(-abs(tstat))
  out$coefficients <- cbind(out$coefficients,tstat,pval)
  dimnames(out$coefficients) <- list(names(obj$par),
                                     c("Estimate",
                                       "Std. Error",
                                       "t value",
                                       "Pr(>|t|)"))
  out$llh <- obj$llh
  out$method <- obj$method
  out$link <- obj$link
  out$call <- obj$call
  
  class(out) <- "summary.zeroinfl"
  out
}

print.summary.zeroinfl <- function(x,
                                 digits = max(3, getOption("digits") - 3),
                                 na.print = "", 
                                 symbolic.cor = p > 4,
                                 signif.stars = getOption("show.signif.stars"), 
                                 ...)
{                               
  cat("Zero-Inflated Model Summary\n")
  cat("---------------------------\n")

  cat("\nCall:\n")
  cat(paste(deparse(x$call),sep="\n",collapse="\n"),
      "\n\n",sep="")

  cat(paste("Total Log-likelihood:",x$llh,"\n"))
  
  cat("\nZero-Inflation Model ")
  if(x$link=="logit")
    cat("was fit with a logit link")
  if(x$link=="probit")
    cat("was fit with a probit link")

  k <- x$k
  
  cat("\nCoefficients:\n") 
  print.coefmat(x$coefficients[1:k,],
                digits = digits, signif.stars = signif.stars, 
                ...)
  
cat("---------------------------------------------------------------------------\n")
  
  if(x$count=="poisson"){
    cat("Count Model (Poisson)\n")
    cat("Coefficients:\n")
    print.coefmat(x$coefficients[(k+1):(2*k),],
                  digits = digits, signif.stars = signif.stars, 
                  ...)
  }

  if(x$count=="negbin"){
    cat("Count Model (Negative Binomial)\n")
    cat("Coefficients:\n")
    print.coefmat(x$coefficients[(k+1):((2*k)+1),],
                  digits = digits,
                  signif.stars = signif.stars, 
                  ...)
    cat(paste("\nTheta =",x$theta,"\n"))
  }
  invisible(NULL)
}

messages.body_plain:
Dear Splus-user,
 
We have put together a package ASSIST, a collection
of R functions for fitting many spline-based
non-parametric/semi-parametric linear/non-linear
fixed/mixed models, including polynomial, periodic,
spherical, thin-plate splines and L splines as well
as smoothing spline ANOVA models. It also coveres some
cases of generalized additive models,  multiple
index models, varying coefficient models, functional
linear models, and self-modeling nonlinear regression
models.
 
 
The package contains five main functions:
 
 1. ssr fits non-parametric regression models for 
 independent and correlated Gaussian data, and for
 independent binomial, Poisson and Gamma data; 
 
 2. slm fits semi-parametric linear mixed-effects
 models; 
 
 3. nnr fits non-parametric nonlinear regression
 models;
 
 4. snr fits semi-parametric nonlinear regression
 models; and
  
 5. snm fits semi-parametric nonlinear mixed-effects
 models. 
 
These extend such existing functions in R (S+) as
smooth.spline, gam, nls, lme and nlme.
 
ASSIST may be obtained at CRAN or
 
 http://www.pstat.ucsb.edu/faculty/yuedong/software
  
Detailed information about these functions and many
examples can be found in the manual of this package,
which, together with an older version based on S+ 2000
for Windows and v3.4 for Unix, can also be downloaded
from the above site. 
 
Comments and suggestions are highly appreciated!

messages.subject: Re: question on nls
messages.body_plain:
My version of S-PLUS has 

> methods("AIC")
     nlme3    nlme3        nlme3     nlme3        nlme3     nlme3
 "AIC.gls" "AIC.lm" "AIC.lmList" "AIC.lme" "AIC.logLik" "AIC.nls"

so I think all you need to do is to call AIC on the fitted object. I
believe that to be true for all versions with nlme3 (which was around in
S+2000) and possibly earlier.

It works essentially as Spencer describes, calling logLik.nls.  (It seems 
to allow for weights in the fit.)

On Wed, 3 Mar 2004, Spencer Graves wrote:

>       Recall that nls assumes normal, independent errors.  Thus, the 
> likelihood is
> 
>       prod( (1/(sigma*sqrt(2*pi))*exp(-0.5*(resid[i]/sigma)^2)). 
> 
> Therefore, the log(likelihood) is
> 
>       (-0.5)*( N*log(2*pi*sigma^2) + sum(resid[i]^2)/sigma^2). 
> 
>       You can somehow get the MLE of "sigma", plug this into this 
> formula, and get the log(likelihood).  The AIC is 
> (-2)*(log(likelihood)+k), where k = number of parameters estimated, 
> including sigma. 
> 
>       I don't know the simplest way to get this, and I don't have time 
> to play with it, but ?nls contains a pointer to ?nls.object.  The latter 
> says it has a component "residuals".  From this, you can compute "sigma" 
> = sum(residuals^2)/N, where N = total number of observations.  NOTE:  
> You want to use the MLE here, not (N-k) for the unbiased estimate. 
> 
>       There is probably a much easier way to get this, but I can't think 
> of it right now. 
> 
>       hope this helps. 
>       spencer graves
> 
> Tropmedres wrote:
> 
> >Hello
> >
> >I am doing the curve fitting using the non-linear regression (nls). I am not
> >sure how to select the best model when I cannot get the AIC as in usual lm,
> >glm, gam model. I cannot use the stepAIC function from the MASS library
> >neither. For the nested models I have been using 'anova.nls with test=chisq'
> >but what about the non-nested models?
> >
> >Thank you in advance
> >
> >Wirichada

Dear Spencer,

The mcheck function comes from Crawley, M.J. (2002) Statistical 
Computing. An introduction to data analysis using S-Plus. Wiley & Sons 
Ltd., NY, USA.

mcheck<-function(obj,...){
rs<-obj$resid
fv<-obj$fitted
par(mfrow=c(1,2))
plot(fv,rs,xlab="Fitted values",ylab="Residuals")
abline(h=0,lty=2)
qqnorm(rs,xlab="Normal scores",ylab="Ordered residuals")
qqline(rs,lty=2)
par(mfrow=c(1,1))
invisible(NULL)
}

Regards,
Chris.

BigM <- function( littleM, n)

      bigM <- matrix(0, nrow=n*nrow(littleM), ncol=ncol(littleM))

Horace W. Tso

Yes the matrix is close to 1 Gb (492^3 x 8 byte ~ 953 Mb). Other than the physical memory, the machine has a 4 Gb swap pagefile. I don't know enough about Windows' memory management to say how swapping works. However, given overhead I'd think S has already spilled over onto the hard drive.

messages.subject: Re: Double-exponential model
messages.body_plain:
Well, I do this kind of analysis all the time in SAS and other programs
(WINNONLIN and WINFUNFIT). I also did some simulation in SPLUS 6.1 and added
10% normally distributed error to the simulated data and fitted the
resulting data using SPLUS. The program worked fine and gave me good
results. 
In this kind of models, there is a problem of parameter identifiablity
(between k1 and k2), termed in pharmacokinetics as "flip-flop" phenomena.
This means that the exponent parameter, say k1 obtained from the data
fitting can be assigned to either k1 or k2 and vice versa and the fit would
be the same. 
I am not exactly sure what problem you are facing. Maybe the model is not be
correct or the data itself has a lot of error that SPLUS is not able to fit
to the model. 
I hope this helps and if the data set is small, I could try and fit it for
you. 

Good luck.

Have you looked at the references on the Help page?  In 
particular, ch. 10 of Chambers, J.M. and Hastie, T.J. (Eds.) (1992). 
Statistical Models in S. (Pacific Grove, CA.: Wadsworth & Brooks/Cole) 
describes algorithm="plinear", which might help you.  Are you familiar 
with the discussion of this type of problem in chapter 5 of Bates and 
Watts (1988) Nonlinear Regression Analysis and Its Applications 
(Wiley)?  There may be better literature available on this problem 
today, but I'm not familiar with it. 

     I learned from Bates and Watts that it is often wise to experiment 
with different parameterizations.  In particular, replacing k2 by 
(k1+exp(ln.kd)) would break the identifiability problem.  I don't know 
how good this is, because I haven't tried it. 

     hope this helps.  spencer graves

messages.subject: Re: Double-exponential model
messages.body_plain:
I don't think this has anything to with identifiablity (between k1 and
k2)..both k1 and k2 are well identified within the double exponential
model..had this been k2=(k3+k4), then you have "indetifiability problem" in
terms of separating k3 and k4. (For details- and approaches to handle this:
go to: http://www.boomer.org/c/p3/c20/c2004.html (although this is in
relation to pharmacokinetic modeling, may be not be helpful for all the
members in the list)

In my opinion, this is the case of-- which part of the equation is trying to
describe the data. Assuming your S-plus code is correct and single
exponential model fits reasonably well, double exponential model SHOULD fit
if you constrain values of k2 and (1-w) as low as possible (conversely,
w~~close to 1). But then I don't understand why do you want to do that....At
the same time, if you have good mechanistic reason to fit double-
exponential model then it would make sense.

For those of you who do pharmacokinetic modeling, this concept comes from
the fact that if you simulate the data with 1 compartment model(~single
exponential model), you can fit the data using 2 compartment model(~double
exponential model) just that the parameters associated with the 2nd
compartment (Q and V2) need to be constrained.

I may be wrong, suggestions are welcome. 

Pravin

Pravin Jadhav

form is like this

x1    y1

y1    x1

x1    y1

x1    y1

x2    y2

y2    x2

should return a value of (x1,y1) and (x2,y2)... In other words, I want to 
find a function f such that f(x_i, y_i)=f(y_i, x_i), but f(x_i,y_i) !=

messages.subject: Re: Double-exponential model
messages.body_plain:
1.  I think I see now the source of your problem:  In 
[~w*exp(-k1*t)+(1-w)*exp(-k2*t)], if w=0, there is no information in the 
data to estimate k1.  In that case, nls may find a singularity and 
refuse to return an answer.  (Similarly, if w=1, there is no information 
to estimate k2.)  In theory, this singularity can be broken by 
specifying an informative prior on k1 and k2.  However, I don't know how 
to do that in "nls", or in any other similar function.  If it were my 
problem and it was important enough AND I could not find another 
function to do what I wanted, I would move to R, where I could modify 
the code for "nls" without worrying about violating Insightful's 
intellectual property rights, and modify "nls" so I could specify an 
informative prior and break this singularity problem. 

     2.  Regarding identifiability, the model 
[~w*exp(-k1*t)+(1-w)*exp(-k2*t)] is symmetric between (w, k1, k2) and 
(1-w, k2, k1).  If k2 is replaced by (k1 + exp(k3)), this symmetry 
disappears.  However, if w = 0 or 1, this reparameterization may not help. 

     hope this helps.  spencer graves

Pravin wrote:

> I don't think this has anything to with identifiablity (between k1 and
> k2)..both k1 and k2 are well identified within the double exponential
> model..had this been k2=(k3+k4), then you have "indetifiability problem" in
> terms of separating k3 and k4. (For details- and approaches to handle this:
> go to: http://www.boomer.org/c/p3/c20/c2004.html (although this is in
> relation to pharmacokinetic modeling, may be not be helpful for all the
> members in the list)
>
> In my opinion, this is the case of-- which part of the equation is trying to
> describe the data. Assuming your S-plus code is correct and single
> exponential model fits reasonably well, double exponential model SHOULD fit
> if you constrain values of k2 and (1-w) as low as possible (conversely,
> w~~close to 1). But then I don't understand why do you want to do that....At
> the same time, if you have good mechanistic reason to fit double-
> exponential model then it would make sense.
>
> For those of you who do pharmacokinetic modeling, this concept comes from
> the fact that if you simulate the data with 1 compartment model(~single
> exponential model), you can fit the data using 2 compartment model(~double
> exponential model) just that the parameters associated with the 2nd
> compartment (Q and V2) need to be constrained.
>
> I may be wrong, suggestions are welcome.
>
>
>

messages.body_plain:
I'm not an attorney, and I'd like to hear an attorney comment on 
this.  It is my understanding that if I can modify anything in S-Plus or 
S-Plus code as long as I don't distribute it publicly, or sell it, or 
deliver it to a client as part of a consulting agreement. 

     Insightful claims copyrights, not patent rights, to S-Plus.  
However, it's not obvious (to me at least) what that covers.  Suppose I 
modify stepAIC in the S-Plus version of MASS, and I sell it or deliver 
it to a client as part of a consultation.  The copyrights to the 
original code are held either by Insightful or by Venables and Ripley.  
In either case, I could theoretically be sued for copyright infringement. 

     The same holds if I modify stepAIC in the R MASS library.  
However, with R, the rules are clear:  I can do anything within the 
limits of the GNU license. 

     Comments? 
     Best Wishes,

     Spencer Graves

messages.body_plain:
Windows XP, SPLUS 6.2 (Rev. date 12 Jan Build 6713), nlme version 3.3.2.

I am trying to understand how to use variance functions in nlme()  I had raised this issue on the list last September but was unable to carry through at that time.

Take the CO2 data set as an example and following Pinheiro and Bates we obtain:

> fm1CO2.lis<-nlsList(SSasympOff,CO2)

> fm1CO2.nlme<-nlme(fm1CO2.lis)

> fm1CO2.nlme

Nonlinear mixed-effects model fit by maximum likelihood

  Model: uptake ~ SSasympOff(conc, Asym, lrc, c0) 

  Data: CO2 

  Log-likelihood: -201.3103

  Fixed: list(Asym ~ 1 , lrc ~ 1 , c0 ~ 1 ) 

     Asym       lrc       c0 

 32.47374 -4.636208 43.54203

Random effects:

 Formula: list(Asym ~ 1 , lrc ~ 1 , c0 ~ 1 )

 Level: Plant

 Structure: General positive-definite

             StdDev   Corr        

    Asym  9.5100137 Asym   lrc   

     lrc  0.1283659 -0.160       

      c0 10.4039458  0.999 -0.139

Residual  1.7663891              

Number of Observations: 84

Number of Groups: 12

messages.subject: Re: Double-exponential model
messages.body_plain:
I presume you are trying to estimate the parameters w, k1 and k2 by maximum
likelihood, and there is constraint that 0 < w < 1.

In that case, I have fitted mixture of exponential distributions to data
using 'nls' or 'ms' (or 'optim' in R). My experience is to re-parameterise w
by exp(a)/(1 + exp(a)), hence 1-w is replaced by 1/(1 + exp(a)), where a in
(-infty, infty). This suggestion was due to Prof. Ripley in his reply to a
similar question I posted in r-help-list quite sometime ago. By removing the
constraint, I found the optimisation routine 'behave' a lot more stablely.

Hope this helps.

Kevin Xie

messages.body_plain:
Pravin, 
Maybe, I did not explain my argument clearly. Hopefully this would help 
Ex.  Lets say the model we trying to fit is a 2 exponential ~w*exp(-k1*t)+
(1-w)*exp(-k2*t)  
Now from the fitting you got the following w=0.6 , k1=0.07 and k2=0.5
This means that the SS function and the fit will be the same if the model
was 
~0.6*exp(-0.07*t)+0.4*exp(-0.5*t) or 
~0.4*exp(-0.5*t)+0.6*exp(-0.07*t)
So without knowing any prior information about k1 or k2 we will never know
what is k1 (in here k1 could be 0.5 or 0.007).
Finally I don't think that parameterization of the model will not help to
solve the identifiablity problem. Simply we need more information about the
system (about k1 and k2). Parameterization/constraining is helpful to
prevent physiologically unrealistic solution (k1~k2). 
I do agree with that a 2 exponential model should fit 1 exponential model. 

Nidal AL-Huniti

-----Original Message-----
From: s-news-owner at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
[mailto:s-news-owner at lists.biostat.wustl.edu] On Behalf Of Pravin
Sent: Thursday, March 04, 2004 7:50 PM
To: 'Nidal AL-Huniti'; 'Eddie Webber'; s-news at lists.biostat.wustl.edu
Subject: Re: [S] Double-exponential model

I don't think this has anything to with identifiablity (between k1 and
k2)..both k1 and k2 are well identified within the double exponential
model..had this been k2=(k3+k4), then you have "indetifiability problem" in
terms of separating k3 and k4. (For details- and approaches to handle this:
go to: http://www.boomer.org/c/p3/c20/c2004.html (although this is in
relation to pharmacokinetic modeling, may be not be helpful for all the
members in the list)

In my opinion, this is the case of-- which part of the equation is trying to
describe the data. Assuming your S-plus code is correct and single
exponential model fits reasonably well, double exponential model SHOULD fit
if you constrain values of k2 and (1-w) as low as possible (conversely,
w~~close to 1). But then I don't understand why do you want to do that....At
the same time, if you have good mechanistic reason to fit double-
exponential model then it would make sense.

For those of you who do pharmacokinetic modeling, this concept comes from
the fact that if you simulate the data with 1 compartment model(~single
exponential model), you can fit the data using 2 compartment model(~double
exponential model) just that the parameters associated with the 2nd
compartment (Q and V2) need to be constrained.

I may be wrong, suggestions are welcome. 

Pravin

Pravin Jadhav

Well, I do this kind of analysis all the time in SAS and other programs
(WINNONLIN and WINFUNFIT). I also did some simulation in SPLUS 6.1 and added
10% normally distributed error to the simulated data and fitted the
resulting data using SPLUS. The program worked fine and gave me good
results. 
In this kind of models, there is a problem of parameter identifiablity
(between k1 and k2), termed in pharmacokinetics as "flip-flop" phenomena.
This means that the exponent parameter, say k1 obtained from the data
fitting can be assigned to either k1 or k2 and vice versa and the fit would
be the same. 
I am not exactly sure what problem you are facing. Maybe the model is not be
correct or the data itself has a lot of error that SPLUS is not able to fit
to the model. 
I hope this helps and if the data set is small, I could try and fit it for
you.

messages.body_plain:
Andy Liaw writes:
> Spencer raised an interesting question (to me, at least):  Am 
> I allow to take an S function that is in the standard S-PLUS 
> distribution and modify it for my own use?

Yes, you can modify S-PLUS code for your own internal use, but you can't then
distribute it to others.

S-PLUS is copyrighted by Insightful. You can only use it if you have a
license for S-PLUS, and you're not allowed to distribute it to others.

That copyright includes the S code you see when you type the name of an S
function at the command line, so if you modify that code, you're allowed to
use it yourself since you have a license for S-PLUS.  But you're not allowed
to then copy that code to others who do not have a license.

Code you write in S entirely yourself is yours: you can do with it as you
wish, and that includes distributing to others under any license you wish (as
many contributors of StatLib have done, for example).

Hope this clears things up.

messages.subject: Re: S-PLUS Vs some other softwares
messages.body_plain:
The problem posed is to find 500,000 regression coefficients,
one for each subject in a large data frame.

Below is a solution that takes 16 seconds in a test problem with
500,000 subjects.  In contrast, the solution mentioned in the 
summary of earlier responses to the question took 19 minutes.

I'll throw in a quick plug for the "Advanced Programming in S-PLUS"
class I'll teach March 18-19 in San Francisco.  Part of what we'll do
is look at ways like this to make S+ run faster.  If interested see:
        http://www.insightful.com/services/schedule.asp

You're trying to do (for 500K patients, roughly 9 rows per patient):

Nsub <- 500000
slope <- rep(0, Nsub)
for(i in 1:Nsub) {
  od.fit <- lm(data.y~data.x, data=data.ram, subset= sub==i, singular.ok=T)
  slope[i] <- coef(od.fit)[2]
}
rbind(slope[1:50], betas[1:50])
# Editorial comment -- I've added spaces for readability.  Please
# do this in postings to s-news.  It is a good habit to follow in general.

# The following solution is based on the formula for the slope coefficient:
#       beta = sum( Y*X ) / sum( X*X )
# where Y = y - mean(y), X = x - mean(x)
# we can simplify further to:
#       beta = sum( y*X ) / sum( X*X )

# Generate some artificial data to test the solution:
set.seed(0)  # for reproducibility
rowsPerPatient <- sample(9, size = 500000, replace=T)
# random number of subjects, including 1, to test robustness of solution
data.x <- rnorm(sum(rowsPerPatient))
data.y <- rnorm(sum(rowsPerPatient))
data.ram <- data.frame(data.x, data.y, sub = rep(1:500000, rowsPerPatient))

#Solution
# For fair comparison with other methods, start with the data frame
# rather than the variables data.x, etc.

# Assume that data.ram is sorted by subject
groupsums <- function(x, counts){
  # sum x by group, where counts contains the size of each group.
  diff( c(0, cumsum(x)[cumsum(counts)]))
}
groupmeans <- function(x, counts){
  groupsums(x, counts) / counts
}
computeBetas <- function(data){
  # assumes names "data.x", "data.y", and "sub"
  counts <- rle(data$sub)$lengths  # equals rowsPerPatient
  x <- data$data.x
  x <- x - rep( groupmeans(x, counts), counts )  # subtract group means
  groupsums(x * data$data.y, counts) / groupsums(x^2, counts)
}
sys.time(computeBetas(data.ram))   # took 15.18 seconds

# My machine is 851 MHz; the 19-minute solution was on a 2 GHz machine.
# Caveat -- my data frame may be smaller, average of 5 rows per patient.

# Check that answers are the same
betas <- computeBetas(data.ram)
all.equal(slope[1:50], betas[1:50])

messages.subject: Re: GAM coefficients and relative risks
messages.body_plain:
Hi
 
It also depends on yor link funktion. But in a traditional poisson log GAM model (which is often used/missused in polution models), the RR found in the literature is calculated by exp(alpha * x_bar) (in a linear model), where alpha is the regression coefficient, and x_bar is the average polutant variable. If its a non-linear model, you could use exp(f(x_bar)), where f(x_bar) is the estimted splime/loess/latent process at the average value of your polutant. I think what is important is that you make clear your reference point, and maybe the median of x is better og the geometric mean.
 
Note that I wirte that the GAM is often missused in polution studies - You can find some arguments the following 
Volume 6. Sven Jesper Knudsen: Bias Adjusted Profile Estimating Functions and State-Space Modeling of Air Pollution Data. Ph.D. Thesis. November 2001
 
which can be downloaded from

http://www.stat.sdu.dk/oldpublications/monographs.html
 
To this is also two s-plus 2000 libraries - KEE and POPKEE for state-space modeling of longterm relative risks and frail population estimation taking harvesting into account. The kee library has  just been converted to s-plus 6, and if you wish, the popkee can (probably) also be converted.
 
Kind Regards
 
Sven

-> "The S-PLUS Language" -> "Syntax of S-Plus Expressions" discusses 
subscripting.  Beyond this, I highly recommend Venables and Ripley 
(2002) Modern Applied Statistics with S, 4th ed. (Springer). 

     "x <- 1:4" will create a vector "x" and store in it the numbers 1, 
2, 3, 4. 

     If you want something more complicated, consider the following: 

     x <- 1:4
     for(i in 2:4) x[i] <- 2+3*x[i-1]

messages.subject: Aggregate bug
messages.body_plain:
Aggregate fails to correctly aggregate certain data frames.  To test, compare the number of unique values in each column of the data frame to be aggregated with the result:

test.aggregate <- function(seed = 1, samp = 1:10, nrow = 1000, ncol = 10) {

        ## tests aggregate()

        set.seed(seed)  

        data <- data.frame(matrix(sample(samp,nrow*ncol,replace = T),nrow = nrow))

        agg.data <- aggregate.data.frame(rep(1,nrow(data)), by = data, FUN = sum)[,1:ncol(data)]

        print(sapply(data,function(x) length(unique(x))) == sapply(agg.data,function(x) length(unique(x)))) ## Compare unique values

        print(c(

                length(unique(apply(data,1,function(x) as.numeric(paste(as.numeric(x),collapse=""))))), ## Actual number of unique combinations

                nrow(agg.data))) ## Number of unique combinations returned by aggregate

        invisible()

}

A correct result comes from:

> test.aggregate(seed = 1, samp = 1:4, nrow = 1000, ncol  = 5)

 X1.1 X1.2 X1.3 X1.4 X1.5 

    T    T    T    T    T

[1] 639 639

But in S-PLUS 6.2 on Windows 2000 for the default values I get the following:

> test.aggregate()

 X1.1 X1.2 X1.3 X1.4 X1.5 X1.6 X1.7 X1.8 X1.9 X1.10 

    T    T    T    T    T    T    T    T    T     F

[1] 1000  200

The 10th column actually contains only 3 unique values.  I narrowed the bug down to

> test.aggregate(seed = 1, samp = 1:9, nrow = 35, ncol  = 10)

 X1.1 X1.2 X1.3 X1.4 X1.5 X1.6 X1.7 X1.8 X1.9 X1.10 

    T    T    F    T    T    T    T    T    T     F

[1] 35 26

Decreasing nrow, ncol or the length of samp will make the bug go away.  Also, changing seed will give different patterns:

> test.aggregate(seed = 2, samp = 1:9, nrow = 35, ncol  = 10)

 X1.1 X1.2 X1.3 X1.4 X1.5 X1.6 X1.7 X1.8 X1.9 X1.10 

    T    F    F    F    F    F    T    T    F     F

[1] 35 17

Are there any other fast implementations of an aggregate like function for S-Plus?________________________________________________________________________

messages.subject: Nested Unbalanced Anova
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-Plus 
Users

 

I am new to S-Plus and so far I 
am using the graphical user interface. After consulting S-Plus help 
files, the archives of this list and Biometry (Sokal & Rohlf) I found 
some info on my problem but some questions remains. I hope some of you can help 
even if its just with a part of the problem it would still be greatly 
appreciated.

 

The story 
goes:

 

I have a unbalanced design in 
which 4 fungal species are represented by a number of different 
cultures which again is replicated 3 times each. Furthermore there are two 
control treatments without fungus, with (3 reps) or without (3 reps) 
phosphorous.

13 different cultures of Fungus 
species A 

5 different cultures of Fungus 
species B

5 different cultures of Fungus species C

2 different cultures of Fungus species D

 

>From the S-Plus help files I 
found that this should be analysed in the linear regression module with cultures 
nested in the fungal species.

 

i.e. 
y~Species/culture

 

However this gives me the 
following error msg. that I dont know what to do about:

 

Problem in lm.fit.qr(unset(x), 
unset(y)): computed fit is singular, rank 26 
Use traceback() to see the call 
stack 

 

Then somewhere in the archives 
(sorry I forgot who it was) I found this error described with the solution that 
the analysis should be performed in the ANOVA module instead and then it should 
work.

 

Doing this, yes I get a result 
but in the report window it prints 
130 out of 156 effects not estimable
Estimated effects may be unbalanced

 and when asking for 
coefficients i get:

Warning messages:
    Design is unbalanced. 
Standard errors are not computed for type = "means" in: 
model.tables(object,
 type = "means", se = T)

So obviously there is a problem 
here. What can I do about this??

At the same time I noticed that similar to Mélanie 
Glaetti (11 sept 2001) from the archives. The ANOVA analysis use 
fungal MS over error MS to calculate the F value instead of nesting culture in 
fungal species and therefore use fungal species MS over culture MS (as described 
in Biometry by Sokal & Rohlf). 

I hope someone can shed light on the reasons why first 
of all the analysis does not run at all when using the linear regression module 
? 

Second, if I can use the ANOVA analysis how do I 
get it to use the right MS and take the unbalanced design into 
account?

Third, do I need 
to specify in my model somehow that it is unbalanced?

Finally, The control treatments 
are not nested in fungal species so should these be omitted from the analysis 
since what I am really interested in is first of all differences between species 
and differences between cultures?

Sorry for this very long question but I am as I already 
mentioned - Desperate.

Any help will be appreciated 

Best regards

Lisa Munkvold
Plant Research 
Department
Risø National 
Laboratory
Denmark

Planteforskning

Frederiksborgvej 399 
P.O.Box 49 - DK-4000 
Roskilde 

Tlf.    : 4677 4210

messages.subject: Re: intellectual property (was: Double-exponential model)
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

You wrote: ``S-PLUS is copyrighted by Insightful. You can only use it if you
have a license for S-PLUS,...''

Can you quote me the U.S. statute which says that?  Though it's been a while
since I read it, as I recall, copyright law governs _distribution_, not
_use_.  The distinction here is that if you have a copy which you have
legitimately acquired, you may allow anyone to use it, so long as you don't
distribute it without the copyright holder's permission.

Your sentence went on to say: ``... and you're not allowed to distribute it
to others.''  I believe that part is correct, and is the only part of that
sentence which is correct.

What you suggested in the first part of that sentence is equivalent to
saying that I can't let anyone else read the newspaper I buy.  So, if you
can quote me the statute which bears out what you said, I'll start lobbying
my congresscritters to get it fixed.

The point I think you were trying to make was that the original questioner
couldn't distribute Insightful's code, even if they had modified it.  That
I'm in complete agreement with; that's a big part of why I choose to use R
instead of S-plus.

Nels Tomlinson

Subject: Re: [S] intellectual property (was: Double-exponential model)

Andy Liaw writes:
> Spencer raised an interesting question (to me, at least):  Am 
> I allow to take an S function that is in the standard S-PLUS 
> distribution and modify it for my own use?

Yes, you can modify S-PLUS code for your own internal use, but you can't
then
distribute it to others.

S-PLUS is copyrighted by Insightful. You can only use it if you have a
license for S-PLUS, and you're not allowed to distribute it to others.

That copyright includes the S code you see when you type the name of an S
function at the command line, so if you modify that code, you're allowed to
use it yourself since you have a license for S-PLUS.  But you're not allowed
to then copy that code to others who do not have a license.

Code you write in S entirely yourself is yours: you can do with it as you
wish, and that includes distributing to others under any license you wish
(as
many contributors of StatLib have done, for example).

Hope this clears things up.

# David Smith

> > refuse to return an answer.  (Similarly, if w=1, there is no

messages.subject: lme
messages.body_plain:
Question on lme for v6.2, WinXp.  I have a longitudinal design.  Subjects (N
= 57) are randomly assigned to one of three treatment programs such that
trt1 (n1 = 20), trt2 (n2 = 16), and trt3(n3 = 21).  The outcome variable is
measured at 7 occasions.  Both time and treatment program are factors in the
model.

Y_ijk = mu + alpha_i + d_ij + t_k + (alpha*t)_ik + e_ijk

 d_ij is a random effect associated with subject j in treatment program i.  

I would like to fit the model with lme.

st.lme <- lme(fixed = outcome ~ ordered(time)*trt.prgm, random = ~
1|trt.prgm/subj, data = st.t, me = 'REML', na = na.exclude, control =
lmeControl(maxIter = 50 , msMaxIter = 50, tol = 1e-6, msTol = 1e-7))
anova(st.lme, type = 'm', test = 'F')

When I fit this model, the denominator df for trt.prgm is 0.  How do I get
the correct df for the denominator? 

Respectfully,

Frank Lawrence

messages.subject: Re: Residuals from logistic regression?
messages.body_plain:
Peng Huang wrote:

> Dear All,
>
>
>
> When I fit a logistic regression, say, using
> out<- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, family =  binomial(link = logit))
> How can I find what type of residuals that out$residuals
> gives me? How can I check (what commend it is) whether
> the model fits the data well? Many thanks!
>
> Peng Huang

Use resid(out, type) instead of out$residuals and see ?residuals.glm for 
details. The default type is "deviance". I think out$residuals stores 
"working" which aren't very useful for most purposes. Also, plot(out) 
will give some default fitted plots for your glm object.

See also Venables & Ripley, Modern Applied Statistics with S 4th edition 
(2003), for a better description of the residuals.

-sundar

messages.subject: Re: Residuals from logistic regression?
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, 9 Mar 2004, Peng Huang wrote:

> Dear All,
> 
> When I fit a logistic regression, say, using
> out<- glm(y ~ x1 + x2, family =  binomial(link = logit))
> How can I find what type of residuals that out$residuals
> gives me? 

By reading the help page ?glm.object linked from ?glm.  (It is the usual 
way, by reading the documentation!)

You would do better to use residuals(out), and select the type you want 
from ?residuals.glm.  I very much doubt that you want out$residuals.

> How can I check (what commend it is) whether
> the model fits the data well? Many thanks!

You can't really.  I am guessing this is Bernouilli data (success/failure,
one trial per case)?  The residual deviance gives you a measure of fit, 
but only you can tell if the fit is good enough for your purposes and this 
measure may not be appropriate (for example if you are doing 
classification you don't need accurate posterior probabilities).

--

messages.subject: Re: AIC and LDA
messages.body_plain:
To define AIC, you would have to define a model and a log-likelihood.
Now LDA is derivable from a multivariate-normal common-covariance model 
for the groups and so you could (fairly easily) write an extractAIC method 
for lda (MASS) and use stepAIC (MASS).

*However* the results would be incredibly sensitive to both multivariate
normality and a common covariance, and no really believes that to be an
excellent approximation to real-life datasets.  I haven't supplied an
extractAIC method precisely because I do not want to encourage the use of
AIC here.  So you can do it, but don't expect it to made easy for you.

For the same reasons, the stepwise tests supplied by e.g. SPSS are not 
supplied in my code.

messages.subject: Re: Strange problem
messages.body_plain:
>i have one fine little script which calls the following,
> 
>BigM <- function( littleM, n)
>{
>      bigM <- matrix(0, nrow=n*nrow(littleM), ncol=ncol(littleM))
>      for ( i in 1:ncol(littleM)) {
>                 bigM[,i] <- littleM[,i]
>      }
>      return(bigM)
>}

The function stacks n copies of littleM, relying on littleM[,i] being
repeated to fill in a whole column of bigM.  (Please document your
functions, to save the reader the work of figuring that out.)

Try this instead:

BigM <- function( littleM, n){
  # littleM is a matrix, n an integer.
  # Result is a matrix with n copies of littleM, stacked by rows.
  littleM[ rep(1:nrow(littleM), n), , drop=F]
}

messages.subject: discriminant function analysis
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to generate a dfa model of my data.  My goal is to identify key 
climatic features associated with the geographical range limit in a 
particular species.  The data consists of the presence/absence of a species 
and environmental characteristics (temperature and ppt of each site).  I 
tried to use code from Venables & Ripley, Modern Appl. Stat, but it doesn't 
work in S+6.1.  I am trying to do these things:

1) figure out whether S+ does stepwise discriminant analysis (or how to do 
this), or if it just uses all of the variables entered

2)  graph the output to visually evaluate the fit (i.e., Figure 11.10 in 
V&R, the 1st and 2nd DF on the axes), rather than generate a huge number of 
plots of all the untransformed variables which is the default plot function

3) determine whether it is a problem that the predictor variables are in 
different units (e.g., temperature and precipitation) or does it 
automatically scale them such that the coefficients represent the correct 
weight in the function?

A more statistical question is whether I should limit the sites considered 
in the model to the sites very close to the range edge, so that the 
function is not biased by an arbitrarily large number of sites well outside 
the range.  If so, how do I do this objectively?

many thanks
Lisa

messages.subject: Re: using apply with matrix multiplication
messages.body_plain:
If I understand what you are trying to do, you are misunderstanding how to 
use apply().

If your data were in a three-dimensional array, you could use apply() for 
this.  However, what I think you want to do is apply your function to each 
block of the dataframe test.df as defined by values of 'id'.  You can do 
this using by():

> by(test.df, test.df[,1], DtWD)

Note that the structure returned by by() here is a list of matrices.

Here is a worked example, with the function cleaned of unnecessary calls to 
cbind() and matrix():

> DtWD <-function(data.df)
+ {
+       D <- as.matrix(data.df[, 2:3])
+       W <- as.matrix(data.df[, 4:8])
+       answer <- t(D) %*% W %*% D
+       answer
+ }
> by(test.df, test.df[,1], DtWD)
test.df[, 1]:11
    X.2 X.3
X.2  15   0
X.3   0   0
-----------------------------------------------------------
test.df[, 1]:15
    X.2 X.3
X.2  15  15
X.3  15  15
>

hope this helps,

Tony Plate

At Thursday 10:16 AM 3/11/2004, you wrote:
> Dear Tony
>
>

> Thank you for taking the time to reply. Your comments and methods have
> helped tremendously. I have quickly run your suggested method here and
> it's working fine. However, I now need to add the resulting matrices
> together. I'm not particularly experienced at dealing with lists. I have
> had a quick try. Will I need to unlist and then somehow add the correct
> elements together? (Obviously I want to avoid loops- which is why I am
> doing this task using matrices )
>
> If you have a few more minutes to help I'd be very grayeful
> Many thanks
> Susan

One easy way to do this is to use my abind() function, followed by either 
rowSums() or apply( , , sum):

> x <- by(test.df, test.df[,1], DtWD)
> abind(x, along=3)

, , 1
    X.2 X.3
X.2  15   0
X.3   0   0

, , 2
    X.2 X.3
X.2  15  15
X.3  15  15
> rowSums(abind(x, along=3), dims=2)
    X.2 X.3
X.2  30  15
X.3  15  15
> apply(abind(x, along=3), 1:2, sum)
    X.2 X.3
X.2  30  15
X.3  15  15
>

The abind() function is available as an R package or from statlib (the same 
function works in both S-plus and R).  However, the versions available 
there are old and don't accept a list argument (you would need to call them 
as do.call("abind", c(x, list(along=3))) to get them to work with list 
x.  The latest version, which does accept a list argument is here:

abind <- function(..., along=N, rev.along=NULL, new.names=NULL,

                  force.array=TRUE, make.names=NULL, use.anon.names=NULL, 
use.first.dimnames=FALSE)

{

    if (missing(make.names) && !missing(use.anon.names))

        make.names <- use.anon.names

    arg.list <- list(...)

    if (is.list(arg.list[[1]]) && !is.data.frame(arg.list[[1]])) {

        if (length(arg.list)!=1)

            stop("can only supply one list-valued argument for ...")

        if (!is.null(make.names) && make.names)

            stop("cannot have make.names=TRUE with a list argument")

        make.names <- FALSE

        arg.list <- arg.list[[1]]

        have.list.arg <- TRUE

    } else {

        if (is.null(make.names))

            make.names <- FALSE

        N <- max(1, sapply(list(...), function(x) length(dim(x))))

        have.list.arg <- FALSE

    }

    arg.list <- arg.list[!sapply(arg.list, is.null)]

    if (length(arg.list)==0)

        return(NULL)

    N <- max(1, sapply(arg.list, function(x) length(dim(x))))

    # N will eventually be length(dim(return.value))
    if (!is.null(rev.along))
        along <- N + 1 - rev.along

    if (along < 1 || along > N || (along > floor(along) && along < 
ceiling(along))) {

        N <- N + 1

        along <- max(1, min(N+1, ceiling(along)))

    }

    # this next check should be redundant, but keep it here for safety...
    if (length(along) > 1 || along < 1 || along > N + 1)
        stop(paste("\"along\" must specify one dimension of the array,",
                   "or interpolate between two dimensions of the array",
                   sep="\n"))

    if (!force.array && N==2) {
        if (!have.list.arg) {
            if (along==2)
                return(cbind(...))
            if (along==1)
                return(rbind(...))
        } else {
            if (along==2)
                return(do.call("cbind", arg.list))
            if (along==1)
                return(do.call("rbind", arg.list))
        }
    }

    if (along>N || along<0)
        stop("along must between 0 and ", N)

    pre <- seq(from=1, len=along-1)
    post <- seq(to=N-1, len=N-along)
    # "perm" specifies permutation to put join dimension (along) last
    perm <- c((1:N)[-along], along)

    arg.names <- names(arg.list)
    if (is.null(arg.names)) arg.names <- rep("", length(arg.list))
    # if new.names is a character vector, treat it as argument names
    if (is.character(new.names)) {
        arg.names[seq(along=new.names)[nchar(new.names)>0]] <-
            new.names[nchar(new.names)>0]
        new.names <- NULL
    }

    # Be careful with dot.args, because if abind was called
    # using do.call(), and had anonymous arguments, the expressions
    # returned by match.call() are for the entire structure
    # E.g., compare:
    # > (function(...)browser())(1:10,letters)
    # Called from: (function(...)  browser())....
    # b()> match.call(expand.dots=FALSE)$...
    # list(1:10, letters)
    # With:
    # > test <- function(...) browser()
    # > do.call("test", list(1:3,letters[1:4]))
    # Called from: test(c(1, 2, 3), c("a", "b....
    # b(test)> match.call(expand.dots=FALSE)$...
    # list(c(1, 2, 3), c("a", "b", "c", "d")

    # Create deparsed versions of actual arguments in arg.alt.names

    # These are used for error messages

    if (any(arg.names=="")) {

        if (make.names) {

            # Create dot.args to be a list of calling expressions for the 
objects to be bound.

            # Be careful here with translation to R --

            # dot.args does not have the "list" functor with R

            # (and dot.args is not a call object), whereas with S-plus, 
dot.args

            # must have the list functor removed

            dot.args <- match.call(expand.dots=FALSE)$... # [[2]]

            if (is.call(dot.args) && identical(dot.args[[1]], 
as.name("list")))

                dot.args <- dot.args[-1]

            arg.alt.names <- arg.names

            for (i in seq(along=arg.names)) {

                if (arg.alt.names[i]=="") {

                    if (object.size(dot.args[[i]])<1000) {

                        arg.alt.names[i] <- paste(deparse(dot.args[[i]], 
40), collapse=";")

                    } else {

                        arg.alt.names[i] <- paste("X", i, sep="")

                    }

                    arg.names[i] <- arg.alt.names[i]

                }

            }

            # unset(dot.args) don't need dot.args any more, but R doesn't 
have unset()

        } else {

            arg.alt.names <- arg.names

            arg.alt.names[arg.names==""] <- paste("X", 
seq(along=arg.names), sep="")[arg.names==""]

        }

    } else {

        arg.alt.names <- arg.names

    }

    use.along.names <- any(arg.names!="")

    # need to have here: arg.names, arg.alt.names, don't need dot.args

    names(arg.list) <- arg.names

    # dimnames.all is a matrix of dimension names: dimnames.all[j,i] is

    # the vector of names for dimension j of arg i

    dimnames.all <- matrix(vector("list", N*length(arg.names)), nrow=N, 
ncol=length(arg.names))

    dimnames(dimnames.all) <- list(NULL, arg.names)

    dimnames.new <- vector("list", N)

    # coerce all arguments to have the same number of dimensions
    # (by adding one, if necessary) and permute them to put the
    # join dimension last
    for (i in 1:length(arg.list)) {
        m <- arg.list[[i]]

        # be careful with conversion to array: as.array converts data 
frames badly

        if (is.data.frame(m)) {

            # use as.matrix() in preference to data.matrix() because

            # data.matrix() uses the unintuitive codes() function on factors

            m <- as.matrix(m)

        } else if (!is.array(m) && !is.null(m)) {

            # make sure to get the names of a vector and attach them to 
the array

            dn <- names(m)

            m <- as.array(m)

            if (length(dim(m))==1 && !is.null(dn))

                dimnames(m) <- list(dn)

        }

        new.dim <- dim(m)

        if (length(new.dim)==N) {

            # Assign the dimnames of this argument to the i'th column of 
dimnames.all.

            # If dimnames(m) is NULL, would need to do dimnames.all[,i] <- 
list(NULL)

            # to set all elts to NULL, as dimnames.all[,i] <- NULL does 
not actually

            # change anything in Splus (leaves whatever is there) and 
illegal in R.

            # Since dimnames.all has NULL entries to begin with, don't 
need to do

            # anything when dimnames(m) is NULL

            if (!is.null(dimnames(m)))

                dimnames.all[,i] <- dimnames(m)[perm]

        } else if (length(new.dim)==0) {

            # do nothing

        } else if (length(new.dim)==N-1) {

            # add another dimension (first set dimnames to NULL to prevent 
errors)

            if (!is.null(dimnames(m))) {

                # dimnames.all[,i] <- c(dimnames(m)[pre], list(NULL), 
dimnames(m))[post]

                # is equivalent to dimnames.all[-N,i] <- dimnames(m)

                dimnames.all[-N,i] <- dimnames(m)

                # remove the dimnames so that we can assign a dim of an 
extra length

                dimnames(m) <- NULL

            }

            dim(m) <- c(new.dim[pre], 1, new.dim[post])

        } else {

            stop(paste("'", arg.alt.names[i],

                        "' does not fit: should have `length(dim())'=",

                        N, " or ", N-1, sep=""))

        }

        if (any(perm!=seq(along=perm)) && !is.null(m))
            arg.list[[i]] <- aperm(m, perm)
        else
            arg.list[[i]] <- m
    }

    # Make sure all arguments conform

    conform.dim <- NULL

    for (i in seq(along=arg.list)) {

        if (!is.null(arg.list[[i]])) {

            conform.dim <- dim(arg.list[[i]])

            break

        }

    }

    conform.dim[N] <- 0

    for (i in seq(along=arg.list)) {

        if (any((conform.dim!=dim(arg.list[[i]]))[-N])) {

            stop("arg '", arg.alt.names[i], "' has dims=", 
paste(dim(arg.list[[i]]), collapse=", "),

                 "; but need dims=", paste(replace(conform.dim, N, "X"), 
collapse=", "))

        }

    }

    # Create arg.dim as a matrix with length(dim) rows and
    # length(arg.list) columns: arg.dim[j,i]==dim(arg.list[[i]])[j]
    arg.dim <- do.call("cbind", lapply(arg.list, dim))

    # find the last (or first) names for each dimensions except the join 
dimension

    if (N>1)

        for (dd in 1:(N-1)) {

            for (i in (if (use.first.dimnames) seq(along=arg.names) else 
rev(seq(along=arg.names)))) {

                if (length(dimnames.all[[dd,i]]) > 0) {

                    dimnames.new[[dd]] <- dimnames.all[[dd,i]]

                    break

                }

            }

        }

    # find or create names for the join dimension

    for (i in 1:length(arg.names)) {

        # only use names if arg i contributes some elements

        if (dim(arg.list[[i]])[N] > 0) {

            dnmN <- dimnames.all[[N,i]]

            if (length(dnmN)==dim(arg.list[[i]])[N])

                use.along.names <- TRUE

            else {

                # make up names for the along dimension

                if (dim(arg.list[[i]])[N]==1)

                    dnmN <- arg.names[i]

                else if (arg.names[i]=="")

                    dnmN <- rep("", dim(arg.list[[i]])[N])

                else

                    dnmN <- paste(arg.names[i], 
seq(length=dim(arg.list[[i]])[N]), sep="")

            }

            dimnames.new[[N]] <- c(dimnames.new[[N]], dnmN)

        }

    }

    # if no names at all were given for the along dimension, use none

    if (!use.along.names)

        dimnames.new[N] <- list(NULL)

    # construct the output array from the pieces

    # don't use names in unlist because this can quickly exhaust memory

    # when abind is called with "do.call" (which creates horrendous names)

    out <- array(unlist(arg.list, use.names=FALSE),

                 dim=c( arg.dim[-N,1], sum(arg.dim[N,])),

                 dimnames=dimnames.new)

    # permute the output array to put the join dimension back in the right 
place

    if (any(order(perm)!=seq(along=perm)))

        out <- aperm(out, order(perm))

    # if new.names is list of character vectors, use whichever are non-null

    # for dimension names, checking that they are the right length

    if (!is.null(new.names) && is.list(new.names)) {

        for (dd in 1:N)

            if (!is.null(new.names[[dd]]))

                if (length(new.names[[dd]])==dim(out)[dd])

                    dimnames(out)[[dd]] <- new.names[[dd]]

                else if (length(new.names[[dd]]))

                    warning(paste("Component ", dd,

                                  " of new.names ignored: has length ",

                                  length(new.names[[dd]]), ", should be ",

                                  dim(out)[dd], sep=""))

    }

    out

}

> list or printout

> > how can she get output of particular quantiles for the data?

> 
> Look at ?boxplot and ?quantile.
> 
> x <- rnorm(100)
> x.bp <- boxplot(x, plot = FALSE)
> x.q <- quantile(x, prob = c(0.01, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.99))
> # print results
> x.bp
> x.q
> 
> -sundar
> (War Eagle)

A subtle point to keep in mind is that the statistics used to generate
boxplots are not really quantiles, even though they should be very close.
They are the `five-number summary' based on `letter values'.  From Sundar's
example you will see that boxplot() returns statistics that are slightly
different from quantile() (using the default prob argument).  In R, there's
a fivenum() function that computes the `right thing' without calling
boxplot(), and it looks like:

> fivenum
function (x, na.rm = TRUE) 
{
    xna <- is.na(x)
    if (na.rm) 
        x <- x[!xna]
    else if (any(xna)) 
        return(rep.int(NA, 5))
    x <- sort(x)
    n <- length(x)
    if (n == 0) 
        rep.int(NA, 5)
    else {
        d <- c(1, 0.5 * floor(0.5 * (n + 3)), 0.5 * (n + 1), 
            n + 1 - 0.5 * floor(0.5 * (n + 3)), n)
        0.5 * (x[floor(d)] + x[ceiling(d)])
    }
}

HTH,
Andy

This is not really an S-Plus question but is much more a question about
statistical methodology.  It would be beneficial to study one or more of
the several books that cover logistic regression, then you'll know how to
proceed.  After reading a bit you'll discover for example that the t
distribution is not appropriate for models that have no error variance
parameter to estimate, and you'll discover how the easy-to-obtain and
often adequate Wald test can help, and when to go to a bit more trouble

messages.subject: Re: cophenetic correlations for dendrograms
messages.body_plain:
There's a cophenetic() function in R, which looks like this:

"cophenetic" <- function (x) 
{
    x <- as.hclust(x)
    nobs <- length(x$order)
    ilist <- vector("list", length = nobs)
    names(ilist) <- 1:nobs
    rmat <- matrix(NA, nr = nobs, nc = nobs)
    for (i in 1:(nobs - 1)) {
        inds <- x$merge[i, ]
        ids1 <- if (inds[1] < 0) 
            -inds[1]
        else ilist[[inds[1]]]
        ids2 <- if (inds[2] < 0) 
            -inds[2]
        else ilist[[inds[2]]]
        ilist[[i]] <- c(ids1, ids2)
        for (ival1 in ids1) for (ival2 in ids2) {
            if (ival1 > ival2) 
                rmat[ival1, ival2] <- x$height[i]
            else rmat[ival2, ival1] <- x$height[i]
        }
    }
    return(as.dist(rmat))
}

As far as I can see, this should work in S-PLUS, except you need to supply
the as.dist() function called in the last line.  The as.dist() in R looks
like:

"as.dist" <- function (m, diag = FALSE, upper = FALSE) 
{
    if (inherits(m, "dist")) 
        ans <- m
    else {
        m <- as.matrix(m)
        ans <- m[row(m) > col(m)]
        attributes(ans) <- NULL
        if (!is.null(rownames(m))) 
            attr(ans, "Labels") <- rownames(m)
        else if (!is.null(colnames(m))) 
            attr(ans, "Labels") <- colnames(m)
        attr(ans, "Size") <- nrow(m)
        attr(ans, "call") <- match.call()
        class(ans) <- "dist"
    }
    if (is.null(attr(ans, "Diag")) || !missing(diag)) 
        attr(ans, "Diag") <- diag
    if (is.null(attr(ans, "Upper")) || !missing(upper)) 
        attr(ans, "Upper") <- upper
    ans
}

This should also work in S-PLUS, if you change the "TRUE" to "T" and "FALSE"
to "F".

HTH,
Andy

                     user which is possible (and desirable to
                     have available as variable names sometimes).
For this reason, logicals *print* as TRUE and FALSE in R
and (because of compactness) as "T" and "F" in  non-R versions of S

R's symnum() function is often overlooked for even nicer
printing of logical objects  (by default as  '|' and '.' for
TRUE and FALSE).

messages.body_plain:
I read a data file into a data frame. Then I tried to have
all the columns in the data frame as non factors (character vectors).

I looped over all columns in the data frame as:

 

for(i in 1:ncol(DF)) DF[,i] <- as.vector(as.character(DF[,i]))

 

But it did not work!

 

Then I used the list representation for columns I know are
factors and it worked, please see this toy example, 

 

> DF <- data.frame(x=1:4, y=c(1, 2, "A1",
"A2"))

> DF

  x  y 

1 1  1

2 2  2

3 3 A1

4 4 A2

 

# Find columns in the data frame that are factors 

> is.factor(DF[,1])

[1] F

> is.factor(DF[,2])

[1] T

 

# I don’t want DF$y to be a factor, just a character
vector, so this is what I used:

> DF[,2] <- as.vector(as.character((DF[,2])))

> is.factor(DF[,2])

[1] T           
#  so it did not work … ??

 

> DF$y <- as.vector(as.character((DF$y)))

> is.factor(DF[,2])

[1] F           
# this one worked …  ??                  

 

Why did this happen?

And if this is an expected behavior, is there a way to make
all columns in a data frame non factors?

 

Thanks for your help.

 

 

Gamal Abdel-Azim, Ph.D.

messages.subject: Logistic Regression
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone, I need help.

I have never used logistic regression before, AND I am new to S-plus.  So, needless to say, I am a little bit lost.

I am modeling DEFAULT as a binary response to RATING (a factor at 9 levels) and SECTOR (a factor at 3 levels).  I have the data formatted and ready to go.  In fact, I even have results from running: fit<-glm(DEFAULT~RATING+SECTOR,family=binomial(link=logit),data="" But, I need a good lesson in how to interpret the results.  I have read several posts including instructions on how to get p-values from the t-stats that summary(fit) produces, and that perhaps Likelihood Ratio tests would be more appropriate if you suspect the Hauck-Donner Effect, etc.  So, my questions are many and perhaps misguided:

1)  I look at the results from summary(fit), and I see that the coefficients matrix has values for RATING1, . . . ,RATING8; and SECTOR1 & SECTOR2.  So, one level of each factor is left out.  My question is: Which level is left out, and how do I know which level is being referred to by RATING1, etc.?  Also, can I still infer anything about the last level?

2)  What are some of the tell-tale signs of the Hauck-Donner Effect?  When should I suspect it?  And, more importantly how do I perform the likelihood ratio tests using S-plus?

3)  The conclusion that I would most like to reach is that SECTOR is not a significant factor in predicting DEFAULT, but RATING is a significant factor.  So, if I have results from summary(fit) that detail each factor at it's different levels, then what is the best way to interpret these results given that I only want to make a broad conclusion?

Any advice would be greatly appreciated!  The more detailed the better!

Thank you all in advance!

Gratefully Yours,

Ryan Schneck

messages.subject: Re: error: too many databases attached
messages.body_plain:
You have not provided enough info for anyone to be very helpful.  Why do you
need to attach() data frame for fitting nls models?  When you attach() a
data frame (or a list), a copy of the object is made and attached.  If you
try to do this in R, you're likely to run into trouble even earlier than in
S-PLUS (depending on the size of the data frames and the available memory on
your computer).  

Do provide a more detail description of what you did and what you are trying
to do, and you're likely to get more informative help.

Best,
Andy

Thanks in advance,

> fisher.exact
function(x, y = NULL)
{
  #       a | b
  #  x = -------
  #       c | d
  if(!is.null(y)) x <- table(x, y) else x <- round(x)
  a <- x[1, 1]
  b <- x[1, 2]
  c <- x[2, 1]
  d <- x[2, 2]
  N <- sum(x)
  p <- dhyper(a, a + b, c + d, a + c)
  x <- seq(max(0, a + b - (N - a - c)), min(a + b, a + c))
  dhyp <- dhyper(x, a + b, c + d, a + c)
  sum(dhyp[dhyp <= p])
}

[1] 0.003818837
>

sure why there is a restriction in fisher.test.

             SUMMER SCHOOL ON IMPRECISE PROBABILITIES

            University of Lugano, Lugano, Switzerland
                        July 27-31, 2004

    http://www.idsia.ch/~zaffalon/events/school2004/school.htm
******************************************************************

ABSTRACT

Imprecise probability is a generic term for the many mathematical or 
statistical models which measure chance or uncertainty without sharp 
numerical probabilities. Imprecise probability models are needed in 
inference problems where the relevant information is scarce, vague or 
conflicting, and in decision problems where preferences may also be incomplete.

The school on imprecise probabilities will offer a wide and deep 
introduction to imprecise probability topics, both theoretical and applied. 
In particular, the school will focus on coherent lower previsions and their 
behavioral interpretation, decision theory, robust statistics, risk 
analysis, imprecise probability methods for artificial intelligence and 
knowledge discovery.

The school is organized by the Society for Imprecise Probability Theories 
and Applications (SIPTA).

------------------------------------------------------------------

INTENDED AUDIENCE

The school is mainly intended for advanced master or Ph.D. students, 
postdoctoral fellows, and junior researchers.

------------------------------------------------------------------

PROGRAM

The school is divided in 5 courses, one per day, of 8 hours each:

probabilities.

messages.subject: Re: help
messages.body_plain:
You need to do a likelihood ratio test: anova will do that for you for glm 
fits.

fit1 <- glm(DEFAULT ~ RATHING + SECTOR, family = binomial)
fit2 <- update(fit1, . ~ . - RATING)
fit3 <- update(fit1, . ~ . - SECTOR)
anova(fit2, fit1, test = "Chisq")
anova(fit3, fit1, test = "Chisq")

Wald tests (and hence t values) are unreliable for logistic regressions.
You also need to think about overdispersion (when you may need test="F").

A slicker way to so this is

drop1(fit1, test="Chisq")

You will find discussion and examples in Chapter 7 of Venables & Ripley 
(2002).
